Picturing Ancient People: Gender in Ancient Greek Vase-Painting

This workshop will take place online. Registration is required; click through for the registration link. Zoom information will be provided via confirmation email to registered participants. Expanding the Ancient World is a series of professional development workshops and online resources for teachers. events.name: Exhibition Lecture: Portable Prayers: Objects, Adornment, and Devotion in Jewish Antiquity
events.description:
Speaker: Karen Stern

This lecture will take place in person at ISAW. Registration is required; click through for the registration link. Conventional studies of ancient Jewish prayer and its evolution focus primarily on recitations or performances of precatory texts, liturgy, or poetry once conducted inside Jewish homes, synagogues, and study halls. This talk adopts a different focus: it considers inextricable connections between the minds, hearts, and bodies of Jewish supplicants and the portable things that they once attached to their bodies with strings and cords, including inscribed amulets and phylacteries of various sorts.

organizer.name: Institute for the Study of the Ancient World

The Bones We Leave Behind: Bioarchaeology and How to Teach It

This workshop will take place online. Registration is required; click through for the registration link. Zoom information will be provided via confirmation email to registered participants. Expanding the Ancient World is a series of professional development workshops and online resources for teachers. This workshop will provide educators with an understanding of what bones can tell us about the past. Participants will learn how parts of who we are get left behind on our skeletons – and how to read them!

events.name: Reconsidering the Rise of a Newly Discovered Iron Age Kingdom in Anatolia:
events.description:
Speaker: James Osborne

Great King Hartapu and the Türkmen-Karahöyük Archaeological Project

This lecture will take place in person at ISAW. Registration is required; click through for the registration link. Since the 2019 discovery of a royal inscription authored by "Great King Hartapu," Iron Age Anatolian scholarship has been energised by the appearance of a hitherto unknown kingdom in the Konya Plain. While the historical context of Hartapu’s inscriptions have undergone dramatic reassessment in light of this new text, little attention has been paid to the conditions that would have contributed to the rise of this kingdom in the first place. This lecture proposes several factors that likely played a role in the emergence of the kingdom: cultural and economic interaction with the Neo-Assyrian Empire, similar relations with Phrygia, emulative competition with its local peer polities and a propitious ecological setting at a time of significant environmental transformations.

events.description: Click here to RSVP Book Presentation An Intellectual against Fascism (2026, University of Toronto Press Lorenzo Da Ponte Italian Library) Selected writings of Piero Gobetti (1901-1926) Translated into English by Sandro-Angelo de Thomasis Edited by Mimmo Cangiano, Davide Dalmas, Sandro-Angelo de Thomasis and Marta Vicari Featuring: Remarks by Sandro-Angelo de Thomasis, The Juilliard School Luigi Ballerini, General Editor, Lorenzo Da Ponte Italian Library A panel with the translator in conversation with: David Forgacs, NYU David Ward, Wellesley College Moderated by Finn Davis, Undergraduate student, Middlebury College In ENGLISH 2026 marks the centenary of the death of Italian journalist, radical liberal, and anti-fascist intellectual Piero Gobetti (1901–26). Today, his insights into liberalism and anti-fascism resonate more than ever, particularly in light of the resurgence of reactionary politics reminiscent of fascism and ongoing debates surrounding (neo-)liberalism. An Intellectual against Fascism offers anglophone readers a new translation of over thirty articles that span Gobetti’s entire journalistic career, half of which have previously been unavailable in English. The volume is thoughtfully organized to allow readers to trace the progressive development of his ideas. To enhance understanding of Gobetti’s thought, this expertly curated collection includes his writings on literature, theatre, and literary criticism. It also features the complete text of La Rivoluzione Liberale (1924), his magnum opus, which has not been available in its entirety before. An extensive critical apparatus accompanies the collection, including a preface, an introduction, and concise introductions and notes for each article.

events.name: Roundtable: Italian Feminism(s)
events.description: Click here to RSVP Roundtable Italian Feminism(s) Words and Voices from a Kaleidoscopic Movement Featuring: Alessandra Abate (Ph.D. Candidate, NYU) on Lea Melandri Serena Bassi (Yale University) on Silvia Federici Alessandro Giammei (Yale University) on Carla Lonzi Diletta Pasetti (Rutgers University) on Gabriella Parca Vanessa Roghi (NYU) on Michela Murgia Moderated by Teresa Bertilotti (Ljubljana University) In ENGLISH How many feminisms have crossed Italy? One distinctive feature of Italian feminism is how personal experience, collective practice, and theoretical reflection have deeply shaped one another, expressing a plurality of perspectives. From the mid-1960s, the movement took shape through various initiatives and often divergent standpoints, from autonomous collectives such as Rivolta Femminile, which practiced consciousness-raising, to Marxist feminist groups that demanded wages for housework, as well as campaigns for abortion and divorce rights and early forms of lesbian feminist organizing. These debates over sexuality, unpaid labor, and civil rights raised questions that still inform contemporary feminist politics. By bringing five figures from different generations and traditions into dialogue–emblems of the many nuances this movement produced–, this roundtable navigates their viewpoints through a conversation rooted in their own words. Starting from their texts, the discussion explores how theorists, activists, writers, and journalists who reflected on body, family, and sexuality drew on their experiences to develop ideas and intervene in public life, raising questions that still resonate today. Because the personal is always political.

events.name: Claude McKay, Wanderings of a Rebellious Poet Virtual Talkback and Film Screening
events.description: Virtual post-screening discussion and Q&A with French director Matthieu Verdeil and distinguished scholar Dr. Robert Reid-Pharr. This program is organized by the Center for Black Visual Culture and co-sponsored by NYU Institute of French Studies and NYU Department of Social and Cultural Analysis. Claude McKay, Wanderings of a Rebellious Poet (52’ - 2025 - english subtitles) film will be shared to all registrants via email with a viewing link, 48 hours in advance of the program. After 48 hours, the film will no longer be available to view. To have access to the film viewing link you must register BEFORE November 27th. Claude McKay, Wanderings of a Rebellious Poet is a captivating voyage through the 1920s — from Harlem to Marseille, via Jamaica, Russia and Morocco — in the footsteps of Jamaican American writer Claude McKay. A rebellious voice of the Harlem Renaissance, Claude McKay spent two decades traveling the world, immersing himself in artistic and political avant-gardes while building an enduring body of work. This remarkable documentary portrait, illustrated with rare archival footage and photographs, narrated by Gaël Faye, and set to a stirring soundtrack, brings his legacy to life. For over 20 years, film director and producer Matthieu Verdeil has pursued a distinctive path at the crossroads of history, memory, and artistic creation. He collaborates with contemporary artists such as Abraham Poincheval while dedicating much of his career to rediscovering overlooked figures and movements in cultural history, including Varian Fry and Claude McKay. Verdeil first became interested in McKay in the early 2000s, recognizing him as both a pioneer of the Harlem Renaissance and a forerunner of global Black consciousness. He began extensive archival research, working with U.S. scholars Brent Hayes Edwards and French publisher Renaud Boukh (Héliotropismes). In 2021, Verdeil directed Claude McKay: From Harlem to Marseille, the first documentary devoted to the “vagabond poet.” Combining historical rigor with poetic sensitivity, the film was screened in France, the United States, Germany, the United Kingdom and beyond. Currently, Verdeil is preparing a new television film dedicated to the Harlem Renaissance, continuing his long-standing commitment to amplifying forgotten or marginalized voices whose legacies continue to shape our present, and to exploring the transatlantic fabric of Black thought. Robert F. Reid-Pharr is a Professor of Social and Cultural Analysis at New York University. He holds a Ph.D. in American Studies and an M.A. in African American Studies from Yale University as well as a B.A. in Political Science from the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. He has been the Jess and Sara Cloud Distinguished Visiting Professor of English at the College of William and Mary, the Edward Said Visiting Chair of American Studies at the American University of Beirut, the Drue Heinz Visiting Professor of English at the University of Oxford, the Carlisle and Barbara Moore Distinguished Visiting Professor of English at the University of Oregon, and the F.O. Matthiessen Visiting Professor of Gender and Sexuality at Harvard University. A prominent scholar in the field of race and sexuality studies, he is the author of four books and numerous essays. His research and writing have been supported by grants from the Mellon Foundation, the National Endowment for the Humanities, the Alexander von Humboldt Foundation, the Radcliffe Institute for Advanced Studies, and the American Academy in Berlin. His work has been honored by the Publishing Triangle, the Modern Language Association and the American Literature Association. In 2015 he was inducted into the Johns Hopkins Society of Scholars and he is the recipient of a 2016 John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation Fellowship.

events.name: Fatal attraction within the DM fluid
events.description: A force acting only on dark matter (DM) cannot be probed in the lab. Yet when it is attractive, and acts coherently across astrophysical distances, it can dominate over gravity even at very weak coupling. Such a force is tightly constrained cosmologically and in the Bullet Cluster, but is harder to detect if its range is limited to sub-galactic scales. In this talk I describe the probes of such short-distance deviations from purely Cold Dark Matter, including CMB lensing and the observed populations of dwarf galaxies. I also discuss concrete realizations of this scenario, finding that the DM invariably sources a background density for the field mediating the new interaction. The enhanced structure growth due to the additional attraction is therefore partially counteracted by the fact that the scalar component does not cluster.

events.name: How Dust Evolution Shapes Protoplanetary Disks
events.description: Planet formation begins with the coagulation of micrometer-sized dust grains in a protoplanetary disk. This particle growth not only provides the building material for planetesimals but also shapes the environments they form in. Aerodynamic drag forces between gas and dust determine how fast the grains drift and how efficiently they can be trapped in the frequently observed rings and vortices in protoplanetary disks. The size of the particles thus affects the available dust mass and composition throughout the disk. Dust also dominates the opacities and therefore regulates the thermal structure and the onset of hydrodynamic instabilities that depend on thermal relaxation. In my talk, I will present two recent applications of coupled multifluid simulations and dust coagulation models that capture the interplay of microphysics and large-scale dynamics in protoplanetary disks: Our simulations of planet-disk systems with dust coagulation quantify the amount of small dust grains that diffuse and drift through planet-induced gaps. These calculations constrain the composition and available mass of solids in the inner disk regions. We furthermore investigate the effects of dust evolution on protoplanetary disk turbulence, induced by the Vertical Shear Instability. Our simulations show that efficient dust coagulation can suppress turbulence in protoplanetary disks, due to the reduced collisional cooling in the dust-depleted upper layers. Understanding how dust coagulation influences the dynamics of protoplanetary disks is thus key to understanding the initial conditions for planet formation and to interpreting multi-wavelength observations.

events.name: Engineering Molecular-spin-based Quantum Technologies
events.description: Molecules are the smallest objects whose structure can be modified for function. Approaches employing molecular systems with “engineered” spin Hamiltonians were among the early proposals for condensed matter implementations of quantum information technologies [1]. We can envisage designing molecular spin systems addressing various challenges in the development of scalable quantum computers, including, for example, the realization of quantum error correction strategies; systems designed to provide multiple quantum states (such as qudits) can host more hardware-efficient protocols than qubit-based systems [2].Using electron-nuclear double resonance, we have explored the implementation of a logical qubit encoded on the four states of a I = 3/2 nuclear spin hyperfine-coupled to a S = 1/2 electron spin qubit; the encoding protects against the dominant decoherence mechanism in such systems, fluctuations of the quantizing magnetic field. We explore the dynamics of the encoded state both under a controlled application of the fluctuation and under natural decoherence processes [3]. Our results confirm the potential of these proposals for practical fault tolerant quantum memories.However, a full implementation of this and related schemes requires projective measurement of the spin qubit, which, generally, remains challenging for molecular candidate systems. events.name: AI-Assisted Physics Research: Experiences and Caveats
events.description: In this talk, I will share my experiences of using AI in theoretical physics research. I will first discuss how the AI chatbox can help understand and push forward a project under human's control. Then, I will discuss how AI agents work, from giving them specific calculation tasks to asking them to explore a vague research idea. I will discuss some difficulties I encountered during this AI-assisted workflow. In particular, sometimes the agent moved away from the physical setting of the project, or continued developing an argument before I understood the previous steps. Based on these experiences, I will discuss how to better work with AI, check its results, and keep track of the direction of a research project. The focus will be on practical research experience rather than the technical details of AI, so no prior knowledge of AI is needed.

events.name: Using Tidal Disruption Events as Probes of Massive Black Hole Formation and Growth Over Cosmic Time
events.description: The tidal disruption of a star that wanders too close to a central black hole is a unique probe of quiescent supermassive black holes lurking in the nuclei of galaxies.  We have demonstrated the ability to discover and spectroscopically classify large samples of tidal disruption events (TDEs) in the optical from the Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF) Northern Sky Survey, with systematic high-energy follow-up with Swift and XMM-Newton. From these efforts, we now know the spectroscopic signatures, multi-wavelength properties, and host galaxy preferences of TDEs, and can begin to use TDEs as powerful probes of massive black hole demographics in quiescent galaxies.  One of the most exciting applications of TDEs is the ability to probe intermediate mass black holes (IMBHs) that are expected to reside in dwarf galaxies, with demographics that encode the seeding mechanism of massive black holes in the early Universe.  I will outline our strategy in the next decade for searching for TDEs across the black hole mass function, and over cosmic time, by extending our sensitivity to TDEs to lower central black hole masses and higher redshifts, by exploiting the discovery power of the next generation of wide-field time domain surveys, including Rubin, Roman, ULTRASAT, and UVEX.

events.name: From Physical Hamiltonians to Quantum Neural Networks and Back
events.description: This talk will review our recent work on exploring the analogy between spin systems and neural networks - classical and quantum. First, a one-to-one correspondence between classical spin models and neural networks (NNs) will be established. Training a NN in this mapping corresponds to a family of Ising spin Hamiltonians parameterized by training time. The Thouless-Anderson-Palmer (TAP) formalism will be used to show that training a NN physically implies the destruction of the spin glass and the emergence of hidden order. A natural quantization of neural networks will be introduced. I will demonstrate its recent successful experimental realization in superconducting and trapped-ion quantum computers. Finally, I will introduce measurement-induced quantum neural networks as the potential near-term case for heuristic quantum advantage on modern-day quantum devices. I'll show preliminary results on the trapped-ion hardware, which allows mid-circuit measurements and feedback crucial for building such networks.

events.name: A Hierarchy of Exact Lower Bounds on the Laughlin Spectral Gap: a Bootstrap Approach
events.description: Although the Laughlin state's ability to qualitatively describe many aspects of the fractional quantum Hall effect has long been clear, a rigorous proof that the parent Hamiltonian (the first Haldane pseudopotential) has a spectral gap in the thermodynamic limit has remained open for over four decades. In this talk, we will discuss our recently developed bootstrap approach to deriving positive lower bounds for the spectral gap on the sphere for arbitrary $N_\Phi$ including in the thermodynamic limit $N_\Phi \to \infty$ [1,2]. Our approach can in principle be generalized to pseudopotentials describing other model wavefunctions such as the Moore--Read state or Read--Rezayi sequence. More generally, this work demonstrates that bootstrap methods can be used to rigorously resolve major open problems in quantum many-body physics.[1] M. G. Scheer, E. Khalaf arXiv:2610.18854 (2026)[2] The Laughlin gap problem was also recently solved in a paper by OpenAI. We emphasize that our work is independent and in many ways preceded the OpenAI result and we will discuss the similarities and differences between the two approaches.

events.name: Emulating the Bose-Hubbard Model with Arrays of Superconducting Qubits
events.description: In this talk, we study the propagation, entanglement, and entropy of quantum information using 3x3 and 4x4 arrays of superconducting qubits that emulate the two-dimensional (2D) hard-core Bose-Hubbard model. The 2D arrays feature site-selective, simultaneous control and readout of all qubits. We highlight several recent experimental demonstrations using these arrays, including quantum random walks, Anderson and Wannier-Stark localization [1], the crossover from area-law to volume-law entanglement [2], the realization of synthetic electromagnetic fields throughout the array [3], and studies of flat-band physics in rhombic lattices [4].[1] npj Quantum Information 8, 35 (2022) | arXiv:2107.05035 (2021)[2] Nature 629, 561-566 (2024) | arXiv:2306.02571 (2023)[3] Nature Physics 20, 1881-1887 (2024) | arXiv:2405.00873 (2024)[4] Physical Review X 15, 021091 (2025) | arXiv:2410.07878 (2024)

events.name: Stochastic Dualities in Active Matter
events.description: First-passage processes and stationary states are traditionally regarded as distinct aspects of stochastic dynamics, governed by the backward and forward evolution equations, respectively. In this seminar, I will discuss how the backward equation can be reinterpreted as the forward equation of a dual stochastic process. This introduces a dual system whose stationary observables can be directly related to first-passage quantities of the original system.I will first discuss the application of this duality formalism to active matter under wall confinement. Using the duality relation, I will show how dynamic adsorption of active particles at confining walls directly encodes splitting probabilities, revealing dynamic adsorption and first-passage properties as complementary manifestations of directional persistence.In the second part of the talk, I will shift from boundary confinement to bulk transport by applying the same duality formalism to effective diffusion in periodic force fields. I will show how the effective diffusion coefficient can be expressed entirely in terms of stationary distributions of the physical and dual systems, providing a new perspective on transport in periodic nonequilibrium systems.

Abstract:  The prologue of the Phaedrus intertwines three distinct discussions: the proper way toexercise the body, the right method for reciting Lysias’ speech, and the just relationship tomyths. These discussions are closely mirrored by the physical journey of the two characters,who walk from the center of Athens to a beautiful countryside setting outside the city walls. Iwill argue that Plato unifies these three thematic strands through the central notion ofexercise—μελέτη.On one hand, the medical theories of Acumenus and Herodicus, and on the other, the rhetoricof Lysias, both prescribe forms of exercise that Plato ultimately rejects. The long walkschampioned by the former and the repetitive recitations demanded by the latter entirelyconsume their practitioners’ time. Consequently, this prevents them from dedicatingthemselves to truly essential pursuits, such as the self-knowledge demanded by the Delphicmaxim.Plato illustrates the rejection of these exercises by having Phaedrus adopt the technical jargonof physicians and rhetoricians, which Socrates then subtly mocks in his responses.Furthermore, the physical postures of the characters—first walking through the countryside,then lying down in the grass—echo this double condemnation of the unsound sophisticationfound in both Herodicus’ medicine and Lysias’ rhetoric. Ultimately, these two flawedpractices serve as the negative counterparts to the genuine Hippocratic medicine and Pericleanrhetoric praised at the end of the dialogue.

Jean WinandWhy Were Classical Authors So Fascinated with Ancient Egyptian Hieroglyphs?

Together with papers addressing both the Egyptian evidence and the Greek and Latin traditions that engaged with Egypt’s writing system, these lectures will frame a three-day conversation on the transformation, interpretation, and cultural mobility of hieroglyphic signs between the seventh century BCE and the fourth century CE.
